robots.name: AgiBot A2
robots.description: AgiBot's full-size humanoid service robot, sold as the A2 and as the A2 Ultra, A2 Lite, A2 Max and A2 Pro configurations the maker's own pages name. The product page names four of the maker's own components — ActionGPT, HIMUS, VectorFlux and RTMOF — and says what each does, and the maker's open-source Link-U OS documents an end-to-end route for training a locomotion policy in simulation and deploying it to a physical A2.
robots.variants: A2 Ultra and A2 Lite on the product page's own parameter table and in AgiBot's store, which sells both with a stated price and an add-to-cart control. The maker's document centre and product pages also name an A2 Max, an A2 Pro, and an A2-W, the last a wheeled dual-arm robot documented on its own page, which this record does not cover.
robots.availability_note: AgiBot's store lists the A2 Ultra and the A2 Lite with a stated price, a quantity control and an add-to-cart button, and states a shipping cost band, with customs duty left to the buyer. The product page itself closes with Contact us and a one-to-one customised-service form rather than a price.

named_models.name: ActionGPT
named_models.role_note: AgiBot's product page says ActionGPT generates human-like natural movements based on voice commands and intent, supporting light operational tasks.

named_models.name: HIMUS
named_models.role_note: AgiBot's product page expands HIMUS as its High-performance Multimodal Mapping System 3D-SLAM algorithm and says the system uses it for L4-level autonomous mobility with low latency and minimal drift in complex, dynamic environments.

named_models.name: VectorFlux
named_models.role_note: AgiBot's product page names VectorFlux as its planning and control algorithm, used with HIMUS for autonomous mobility.

named_models.name: RTMOF
named_models.role_note: AgiBot's product page expands RTMOF as its Real-Time Robust Motion Framework, says it applies non-linear model predictive control together with reinforcement learning algorithms and a dynamic planning engine, and says the result quickly generates globally optimal trajectories and improves motion strategies in uncertain environments.

hardware.sensors: An interactive screen, LiDAR, a microphone, a dexterous hand, two RGB-D cameras, a fisheye camera, a speaker, and force/torque sensors. The A2 Ultra page's parameter table lists a 3D LiDAR and an RGB-D camera under its perception system.
hardware.actuation: 40 degrees of freedom plus active DoF, on what the page calls a universal humanoid skeletal structure with a modular design and customizable exterior options. The page says the self-developed integrated joint delivers peak torque of 512 Nm. The A2 Ultra page's table gives the A2 Ultra as 40 total DoF with 2 neck, 7 per arm, 6 per leg, and a 6-DoF dexterous hand.
hardware.power: A 700 Wh battery with about 2 hours of runtime and battery-swapping support.

robots.developer_access: AgiBot's own open-source Link-U OS documents a route for running the reader's own policy on the A2. Its Link-U OS Alpha documentation states the platform is based on the production-proven full-size Agibot Expedition A2, gives an all-in-one toolchain on MuJoCo and Isaac Gym covering training, simulation verification and real robot deployment, trains locomotion with PPO, and states that a single policy codebase runs across MuJoCo simulation and real robots. Its deployment guide targets the Agibot Expedition A2 Flagship Edition, and its rl_deploy repository publishes an aimrl_sdk Python package that streams observation frames from the arm, leg and IMU topics and publishes joint commands for Python-side policy deployment. The guide's user levels name hardware developers with A2 robots for hands-on development and verification. No X2 or A3 equivalent was found.
robots.terms_note: AgiBot's store publishes Terms of Service last updated 2026-02-04, covering access, payment, shipping, returns and liability, alongside separate shipping, refund and privacy policies. No SDK or software licence for the A2 was found at review time; the maker's open-source Link-U OS carries its own Mulan PSL v2 licence, which the maker's product pages do not reference.
robots.not_verified: The four named components and the Link-U OS policy route are AgiBot's own claims; the Atlas has not verified them. Every source is an AgiBot web page or a repository file AgiBot can change at any time.

robots.name: Stretch 4
robots.description: Hello Robot's mobile manipulator, a wheeled base carrying a telescoping lift, a single arm, and a head, sold as a research and commercial platform. Its own documentation ships a grasping demo that runs two named third-party models, and its ROS 2 packages and Python bridge are published open source.
robots.availability_note: Hello Robot's purchase page states a price of $29,950, accepts payment by check, wire transfer, or purchase order, and says Stretch 4 typically ships within two to four weeks of receiving a purchase order or pre-payment.

named_models.name: Molmo 2
named_models.role_note: Hello Robot's grasping demo says perception uses the Molmo 2 Vision-Language Model to output pixel coordinates for a target object described with text.

named_models.name: SAM 2
named_models.role_note: Hello Robot's grasping demo says SAM 2 segments the target object from Molmo 2's pixel coordinates and then tracks and segments that object over time.

hardware.compute: An NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX installed within the base with 128GB NVMe and 16GB memory, with its own WiFi and Ethernet networking to the main compute. Hello Robot sells the Jetson Orin NX as an accessory described as running your AI models on-robot.
hardware.sensors: A head sensor suite of two hemispherical 3D LiDARs covering 360 by 189 degrees at over 2,000,000 measurements per second, two global-shutter RGB cameras of 2.3 megapixels calibrated to the LiDARs for RGBD data, and a 12-megapixel RGB teleoperation camera. The wrist carries an OAK-D SR camera at the roll joint, and the base carries six laser line sensors for cliff and hazard monitoring.
hardware.actuation: A 3-omniwheel holonomic drive with three 8-inch omniwheels, a lift driven by a closed-loop stepper motor through a low gear-ratio belt drive, a single arm, and a 3-degree-of-freedom internally cabled wrist with yaw, pitch, and roll. Hello Robot states a maximum payload of 4 kg retracted and 2.5 kg extended, and that the robot weighs about 60 pounds without its battery.
hardware.power: A removable battery accessed by removing the base's top shell, weighing 30 pounds, with a barrel-jack charge port that Hello Robot restricts to its own 36V charger. The purchase page sells a LiFePO4 25.6V 20A 512W spare battery and ballast, and a docking station with three reflective ArUco tags that the robot uses to dock itself for wireless charging.

robots.developer_access: Hello Robot publishes the robot's ROS 2 packages, including stretch_core, stretch_description, stretch_deep_perception, stretch_nav2, and a stretch_python_bridge package that gives synchronous Python access to ROS 2 image, pointcloud, transform, camera-info, and IMU topics as NumPy arrays. Its product page lists open-source ROS 2 and a Python SDK among the platform's highlights, and its documentation describes reference demos for autonomy and Embodied AI.
robots.terms_note: Hello Robot's Terms of Sale cover its robots, components, and accessories, including shipping and delivery, returns within 30 days of delivery in the contiguous United States and 28 days internationally with a 10% restocking fee, and a one-year limited product warranty from delivery that excludes damage from use other than the product's intended purpose and in accordance with Hello Robot documentation. The purchase page states a 30-day return policy and a limited one-year warranty, and offers an extended three-year warranty and a Full Robot Refurb option. No separate software or SDK licence page was found at review time.

terms_evidence.scope: Terms of Sale covering robots, components, and accessories

robots.not_verified: The named models and the ROS 2 and Python routes are Hello Robot's own claims; the Atlas has not verified them. Every source is a Hello Robot web page or a file in a repository Hello Robot can change at any time.

robots.name: Figure 03
robots.description: Figure AI's third-generation humanoid robot, which Figure says is designed for household tasks and built around Helix, its vision-language-action model.
robots.availability_note: Figure's site offers no way to order Figure 03 and describes no pilot programme. Its news pages describe factory deployments instead: Figure 03 arrived at BMW Group Plant Spartanburg in 2026, after Figure 02 contributed to the assembly of 30,000 cars at BMW the year before.

named_models.name: Helix
named_models.role_note: Figure says Helix controls the full loop of perception, movement, and reasoning, on board and in real time, and that it outputs high-rate continuous control of the entire humanoid upper body, including wrists, torso, head, and individual fingers.

named_models.name: Helix 02
named_models.role_note: Figure's BMW deployment page calls Helix 02 its proprietary pixels-to-actions VLA and says it coordinates Figure 03's hands, arms, torso, and feet, letting the robot manipulate parts while stepping and repositioning its body.

hardware.sensors: A camera system that Figure says delivers twice the frame rate, one-quarter the latency, and a 60% wider field of view per camera, a palm camera in each hand, and fingertip tactile sensors that detect forces as small as three grams. An upgraded audio system has a repositioned microphone.
hardware.actuation: Electric. Figure says the actuators perform at 2x faster speeds with improved torque density; the product page lists a 20 kg payload and a speed of 1.2 m/s.
hardware.power: A battery certified to the UN38.3 standard, with a 5-hour runtime on the product page. Charging coils in the robot's feet let it step onto a wireless stand and charge at 2 kW.

robots.developer_access: Figure documents no SDK, API or programme for running your own model on Figure 03.
robots.terms_note: The only terms page on figure.ai, last updated February 01, 2023, governs use of the figure.ai website and says nothing about the robot's sale, software, or warranty.
robots.not_verified: Helix, and what it does on the robot, is Figure's own claim; the Atlas has not verified it. Every source is a Figure web page that Figure can change at any time.

robots.name: NEO
robots.description: 1X's humanoid robot for the home, built to take on household chores. 1X names the models that run it, Redwood AI and the 1X World Model, and says what each does.
robots.availability_note: 1X takes pre-orders on its order page against a fully refundable deposit and says US deliveries start in 2026. The order page offers NEO either as a monthly subscription or to own.

named_models.name: Redwood AI
named_models.role_note: 1X calls Redwood AI NEO's vision language model for learning and performing chores around the house, and says it is the AI model that lets NEO help around the home, moving, perceiving, and interacting with the world autonomously. 1X also says Redwood is among the first VLAs to control locomotion jointly with manipulation.

named_models.name: Redwood AI reinforcement-learning controller
named_models.role_note: 1X says Redwood AI's latest reinforcement-learning controller gives NEO its mobility: walking in any direction, sitting, standing, kneeling, and climbing stairs using stereo vision.

named_models.name: 1X World Model
named_models.role_note: 1X says the 1X World Model lets NEO anticipate the outcomes of robot actions and their consequences on the world, and that it now serves as NEO's cognitive core, letting it generalise to tasks it has not seen.

hardware.compute: A 1X NEO Cortex chipset (Nvidia Jetson Thor), which the product page rates at up to 2070 FP4 TFLOPS of AI compute.
hardware.sensors: Dual 8.85MP 90Hz stereo fisheye cameras, four beamforming microphones, and linkwise differential IMUs.
hardware.actuation: Low-inertia tendon drives, which 1X calls 1X Tendon Drive. The product page lists 22 degrees of freedom in each hand, 7 in each arm, 3 in the neck, 2 in the spine, and 6 in each leg, with a walking speed of 1.4 m/s.
hardware.power: An 842 Wh battery with a 4-hour run time. 1X says NEO plugs itself in when it needs a charge, and that a quick charge takes 6 minutes per hour of run time.

robots.developer_access: 1X documents no way to run your own model or policy on NEO.
robots.terms_note: The legal page publishes 1X's Pre-Order Terms. They say a buyer who is invited to order must agree to Terms of Sale that are presented at the time of purchase, so the full sale terms are not published ahead of an order. The Terms of Use link, 1x.tech/terms-and-conditions, returned a 404 at review. The order page names a 3-year warranty with the ownership option.

terms_evidence.scope: Pre-order terms on the legal page

robots.not_verified: The models named here, and what they do, are 1X's own claims; the Atlas has not verified them. Every source is a 1X web page that 1X can change at any time.

robots.name: Spot
robots.description: Boston Dynamics' legged robot for automated sensing, inspection, and data capture. Its SDK documents a way to run your own trained model with Spot, and Boston Dynamics says it has built reinforcement learning into Spot's walking control.
robots.availability_note: Spot is sold through Boston Dynamics' sales team: the Spot sales page asks buyers to contact the team to find the right implementation for their application.

named_models.name: Reinforcement-learning locomotion controller
named_models.role_note: Boston Dynamics says it has integrated reinforcement learning into Spot's locomotion control system, which has historically used model predictive control.

hardware.sensors: Terrain sensing with a 360° horizontal field of view and a 4 m range, and built-in stereo cameras. The optional arm's gripper adds time-of-flight, IMU, and 4K RGB sensors.
hardware.actuation: A maximum speed of 1.6 m/s, a 300 mm maximum step height, and a 14 kg payload limit. The optional arm has six degrees of freedom plus a gripper, reaches 984 mm at full extension, and lifts up to 11 kg.
hardware.power: A 564 Wh battery with an average run time of 90 minutes and a 60-minute recharge. Missions can be launched from the Spot Dock.

robots.developer_access: The Spot SDK's Python client library can control Spot and read its sensor and health information. Its network compute bridge runs a model you have trained on a compute payload or a networked server, and your script commands the robot with the results. The Joint Control API, a beta that needs a special-permissions licence, streams low-level joint commands. Boston Dynamics' own demo drove Spot with Google's Gemini Robotics-ER 1.5 through the SDK.
robots.terms_note: The Spot SDK ships under Boston Dynamics' own Software Development Kit License. The website's Terms of Use say Boston Dynamics' obligations for its products are governed solely by the agreements under which they are provided, and those purchase agreements are not published. The specification sheet mentions a one-year limited warranty.
robots.not_verified: The reinforcement-learning controller and the SDK's model interfaces are Boston Dynamics' own claims; the Atlas has not verified them. Every source is a Boston Dynamics web page or repository file that Boston Dynamics can change at any time.

robots.name: Unitree G1
robots.description: Unitree's humanoid robot, sold in a basic version and an EDU version for secondary development. Unitree names UnifoLM-VLA-0, a vision-language-action model built with G1 data, and publishes code for training a policy and deploying it to the robot.
robots.variants: G1 and G1 EDU on the product page, which lists secondary development for the EDU version only; Unitree's shop also offers a G1 Pro option, which it does not describe.
robots.availability_note: Unitree's shop sells the G1 and says it is backordered and will ship as soon as it is back in stock. The shop says that version does not support secondary development; the EDU version is bought by contacting Unitree's sales team.

named_models.name: UnifoLM-VLA-0
named_models.role_note: Unitree describes UnifoLM-VLA-0 as a vision-language-action large model in the UnifoLM series, designed for general-purpose humanoid robot manipulation; the twelve datasets its repository lists for its experiments were all recorded on the Unitree G1.

hardware.compute: An 8-core high-performance CPU. For the EDU version the product page lists a high computing power module, such as Orin, as an accessory.
hardware.sensors: A depth camera and 3D LiDAR, a four-microphone array, and dual joint encoders. The EDU version's optional Dex3-1 hand can carry tactile sensor arrays.
hardware.actuation: Low-inertia, high-speed internal-rotor permanent magnet synchronous motors on industrial-grade crossed roller bearings: 23 degrees of freedom on the basic G1 and 23 to 43 on the EDU version, which offers the force-controlled three-fingered Dex3-1 hand as an option.
hardware.power: A quick-release 13-string lithium smart battery (9000mAh) with about 2 hours of battery life, and a 54V 5A charger.

robots.developer_access: The product page lists secondary development for the G1 EDU only. Unitree's unitree_rl_gym repository documents training a policy in simulation and deploying it to a physical G1 for motion control, and its unitree_ros2 repository documents controlling the robot directly with ROS 2 messages, without wrapping the SDK interface.
robots.terms_note: Unitree's SDK, unitree_sdk2, is released under the BSD 3-Clause License. Unitree's terms page has Terms, After-sales Terms, Privacy Policy, Disclaimer, and End User License Agreement tabs; the after-sales tab is the hardware warranty policy, and the licence agreement is offered as a downloadable document rather than as page text. The product page lists an 8-month warranty for the G1 and 18 months for the EDU version.
robots.not_verified: UnifoLM-VLA-0 and the documented policy interfaces are Unitree's own claims; the Atlas has not verified them. Every source is a Unitree web page or repository file that Unitree can change at any time.

robots.name: Unitree Go2
robots.description: Unitree's quadruped robot dog, sold in AIR, PRO, X and EDU configurations. Unitree names no learned model for it; its robotics repositories document training a reinforcement-learning policy in simulation and deploying it to a physical Go2 for motion control, and controlling it directly with ROS 2 messages.
robots.variants: Go2 AIR, PRO, X and EDU on the product page. Full secondary development is an EDU-only feature, with partial support on the X and none on the AIR or PRO.
robots.availability_note: Unitree's shop sells the Go2 with an add-to-cart button and says orders ship within one month. The EDU version is bought by contacting Unitree's sales team.

hardware.compute: An 8-core high-performance CPU, which the product page says supports advanced, AI, and 3D-mapping modes. A high-computing-power module such as Orin is listed as an accessory.
hardware.sensors: Unitree's self-developed 4D LiDAR L2 with 360-by-96-degree hemispherical coverage and a 0.05 m minimum detection distance, an HD wide-angle camera, and a wireless vector positioning module on the PRO and above. The EDU version adds a foot-end force sensor.
hardware.actuation: Twelve joint motors with about 45 N·m peak joint torque. The product page lists payloads of about 7 to 8 kg, up to 10 to 12 kg maximum by configuration, and speeds up to 2.5 to 3.7 m/s, about 5 m/s maximum in lab tests.
hardware.power: An 8000 mAh smart battery with a 15000 mAh long-endurance option. The product page lists about 1 to 2 hours of battery life, about 2 to 4 on the EDU version, with a fast charger for the EDU.

robots.developer_access: Unitree's unitree_rl_gym repository documents training a reinforcement-learning policy in simulation and deploying it to a physical Go2 for motion control, and its unitree_ros2 repository documents controlling the Go2 directly with ROS 2 messages, without wrapping the SDK interface. The product page gates full secondary development to the EDU version.
robots.terms_note: Unitree's SDK, unitree_sdk2, is released under the BSD 3-Clause License. Unitree's terms page has Terms, After-sales Terms, Privacy Policy, Disclaimer, and End User License Agreement tabs; the after-sales tab is the hardware warranty policy. The product page lists a 6-month warranty for the AIR and 12 months for the other configurations.
robots.not_verified: The documented policy interfaces are Unitree's own claims; the Atlas has not verified them. Every source is a Unitree web page or repository file that Unitree can change at any time.

robots.name: Unitree H1
robots.description: Unitree's full-size universal humanoid robot, sold as the H1 and H1-2. Unitree names no learned model for it; its robotics repositories document training a reinforcement-learning policy in simulation and deploying it to a physical H1 for motion control, and controlling it directly with ROS 2 messages.
robots.variants: H1 and H1-2 on the product page, which lists user-development computing for both.
robots.availability_note: Unitree's shop lists the H1 with an add-to-cart button. Buyers who want product information are told to contact Unitree directly.

hardware.compute: A standard configuration of an Intel Core i5 for platform functions and an Intel Core i7 for user development, with optional modules such as Orin NX.
hardware.sensors: 3D LiDAR plus a depth camera, which Unitree says gives 360-degree depth perception.
hardware.actuation: Low-inertia high-speed internal-rotor permanent magnet synchronous motors on industrial-grade crossed roller bearings. The H1 stands about 180 cm, weighs about 47 kg, and moves at 3.3 m/s with five degrees of freedom per leg and four expandable degrees per arm. The H1-2 stands about 178 cm, weighs about 70 kg, and has 27 degrees of freedom in total, with shoulder and elbow joints of about 120 N·m, wrists of about 30 N·m, and a rated arm load of about 7 kg.
hardware.power: A quickly replaceable 15 Ah (0.864 kWh) battery at up to 67.2 V.

robots.developer_access: Unitree's unitree_rl_gym repository documents training a reinforcement-learning policy in simulation and deploying it to a physical H1 or H1-2 for motion control, and its unitree_ros2 repository documents controlling the H1 directly with ROS 2 messages, without wrapping the SDK interface.
robots.terms_note: Unitree's SDK, unitree_sdk2, is released under the BSD 3-Clause License. Unitree's terms page has Terms, After-sales Terms, Privacy Policy, Disclaimer, and End User License Agreement tabs; the after-sales tab is the hardware warranty policy, and it excludes damage caused by the user's own developer-mode programs from free warranty. The H1 product page states no warranty period.
robots.not_verified: The documented policy interfaces are Unitree's own claims; the Atlas has not verified them. Every source is a Unitree web page or repository file that Unitree can change at any time.

robots.name: Unitree H2
robots.description: Unitree's full-size humanoid robot, sold as the H2 and the H2 EDU. Unitree names no learned model for it; its product page says a 2070 TOPS chip supports diverse intelligent models, and its reinforcement-learning repository lists the H2 among the robots it supports and registers velocity-tracking tasks for it.
robots.variants: H2 and H2 EDU on the product page, which lists secondary development for the EDU version only. Unitree publishes an H2 Plus on a product page of its own, which this record does not cover.
robots.availability_note: Unitree's product page states a price for the H2 and lists the H2 EDU as contact sales. The shop page carries the same price but shows no add-to-cart control, marks the base variant out of stock, and offers a Contact Sales button as its only route to a price.

hardware.compute: Two PC slots, an Intel Core i5 for platform capabilities and an Intel Core i7 for custom development. The product page's description says a 2070 TOPS chip powers the robot, and a high-power computing module is an accessory, with multiple brands and models available such as Thor.
hardware.sensors: A humanoid binocular camera with a wide field of view, and a voice-interaction array of microphone and high-power speaker. WiFi 6 and Bluetooth 5.2 are listed as present.
hardware.actuation: Low-inertia high-speed internal-rotor permanent magnet synchronous motors on industrial-grade crossed roller bearings, with 31 degrees of freedom in total: six per leg, seven per arm, three at the waist, and two at the head. The page states a maximum arm-joint torque of 120 N·m and leg-joint torque of 360 N·m, an arm payload peaking at about 15 kg and rated at about 7 kg, a standing size of 1820 x 456 x 218 mm, a weight of about 70 kg with battery, a calf-plus-thigh length of 1045 mm and a forearm-plus-upper-arm length of 690 mm, and a body of aircraft-grade aluminium, titanium alloy, and high-strength engineering plastics. A bionic head with facial features and dexterous hands in several models are listed.
hardware.power: A premium lithium battery with low internal resistance, 15 Ah (0.972 kWh) at up to 75.6 V, with about three hours of battery life. A quick-release smart battery and a charger are accessories, and cooling is local air cooling.

robots.developer_access: Unitree's product page lists secondary development for the H2 EDU and points to a secondary development manual. Its unitree_rl_mjlab repository names the H2 among the robots it supports, registers Unitree-H2-Flat and Unitree-H2-Rough velocity-tracking tasks, and documents a Train, Play, Sim2Real workflow that deploys trained policies to physical Unitree robots, worked through on the G1. Its unitree_sdk2 repository ships an h2 example directory with low-level joint commands published on rt/lowcmd for the robot's 31 motors and a high-level locomotion client, and its unitree_ros2 repository ships an h2 example that drives H2 ankle commands with ROS 2 messages.
robots.terms_note: Unitree's SDK, unitree_sdk2, is released under the BSD 3-Clause License. Unitree's terms page has Terms, After-sales Terms, Privacy Policy, Disclaimer, and End User License Agreement tabs; the after-sales tab is the hardware warranty policy, and the licence agreement is offered as a downloadable document rather than as page text. The product page lists an 8-month warranty for the H2 and 12 months for the H2 EDU.
robots.not_verified: The documented policy interfaces are Unitree's own claims; the Atlas has not verified them. Every source is a Unitree web page or repository file that Unitree can change at any time.

robots.name: Unitree R1
robots.description: Unitree's compact humanoid robot, sold as the R1 AIR, R1, and R1 EDU, which Unitree's own site lists under its Humanoid Robot category. Unitree names no learned model for it: the product page says it integrates a large multimodal model for voice and image processing without naming one. Its product page states that the R1's joint and sensor control interfaces are fully open, and its reinforcement-learning repository registers a velocity-tracking task for the R1 and ships a deployment program for it.
robots.variants: R1 AIR, R1, and R1 EDU on the product page, which lists secondary development for the R1 EDU only. The shop sells the R1 AIR and R1 in white and red, and takes the R1 EDU by contacting sales.
robots.availability_note: Unitree's product page lists the R1 AIR, R1 and R1 EDU, with the EDU marked contact sales. The shop page shows an add-to-cart control and says the R1 Air (White) is backordered and will ship as soon as it is back in stock.

hardware.compute: An 8-core high-performance processor. A high-power computing module is an accessory of the R1 EDU, with multiple brands and models available such as Orin (40-100 TOPS).
hardware.sensors: A four-microphone array and a speaker, with a monocular camera on the R1 AIR and a binocular camera on the R1 and R1 EDU. WiFi 6 and Bluetooth 5.2 are listed as present, and the page describes a two-degree-of-freedom head for environmental perception.
hardware.actuation: Low-inertia high-speed internal-rotor permanent magnet synchronous motors on crossed roller bearings and double-hook ball bearings. The page lists 20 degrees of freedom on the R1 AIR, 26 on the R1, and 26 to 40 on the R1 EDU, made up of six per leg, four or five per arm, two at the waist, and two at the head. It states an arm load of about 2 kg, a standing size of 1230 x 357 x 190 mm, a weight of about 27 kg with battery on the AIR and about 29 kg on the others, a calf-plus-thigh length of 600 mm and a forearm-plus-upper-arm length of 420 mm, knee motion from -10 to +139 degrees, hip yaw of plus or minus 157 degrees, pitch of -168 to +146 degrees and roll of -60 to +100 degrees, and waist yaw of plus or minus 150 degrees and roll of plus or minus 30 degrees. Electrical routing is hollow plus internal routing and the joint encoders are dual plus single.
hardware.power: A lithium battery with about one hour of battery life. A quick-release smart battery and a charger are accessories, and cooling is local air cooling.

robots.developer_access: Unitree's product page states that the R1's joint and sensor control interfaces are fully open and that mainstream simulation platforms are supported, and lists secondary development for the R1 EDU. Its unitree_rl_mjlab repository names the R1 among the robots it supports, offers a Unitree-R1-Flat velocity-tracking task, and carries a deploy/robots/r1 program with a velocity policy configuration, documented through the same Train, Play, Sim2Real workflow. Its unitree_sdk2 repository ships an r1 example directory with low-level joint examples, a high-level locomotion client, and an audio client.
robots.terms_note: Unitree's SDK, unitree_sdk2, is released under the BSD 3-Clause License. Unitree's terms page has Terms, After-sales Terms, Privacy Policy, Disclaimer, and End User License Agreement tabs; the after-sales tab is the hardware warranty policy, and the licence agreement is offered as a downloadable document rather than as page text. The product page lists a 6-month warranty for the R1 AIR, 8 months for the R1, and 12 months for the R1 EDU.
robots.not_verified: The documented policy interfaces are Unitree's own claims; the Atlas has not verified them. Every source is a Unitree web page or repository file that Unitree can change at any time.
